planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: This European mountain-woodland saxifrage forms a low, spreading mat of small, glossy, wedge-shaped evergreen leaves with scalloped edges, each tapering neatly to the stalk. In late spring, slender branched stems rise just above the foliage carrying loose clusters of small white, star-shaped flowers. It spreads gradually by short stolons to form a tidy groundcover rather than an aggressive one, making it well suited to woodland edges, shaded rock garden crevices, or the front of a shaded border. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil, since it resents both prolonged drought and waterlogging.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade, such as beneath deciduous trees or along a shaded streambank.

directions: Native to shaded mountain woodlands and ravines across southern and central Europe, this species forms a basal rosette of broad, rounded, toothed leaves that give it its name. In early summer it sends up airy, branching flower stems well taller than the foliage, bearing loose sprays of small white flowers dotted with red or yellow spots. It is more upright and open in habit than mat-forming saxifrages, reading more like a dainty woodland wildflower than a groundcover. Plant it in rich, humusy soil that stays reliably moist, since it comes from naturally damp, shaded ravine habitats and does not tolerate dry shade well.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade, where it is sheltered from winter wet.

directions: This Japanese woodland species is the wild parent of the more widely grown Saxifraga fortunei-type cultivars, and shares their rounded, lobed, glossy leaves and late, airy display. In autumn, branching flower stems carry open sprays of white flowers whose lower two petals are noticeably longer than the upper three, giving each bloom a lopsided, fluttering look. It is a welcome late-season bloomer for the shaded garden, picking up momentum just as most other woodland perennials are fading. Grow it in cool, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture through summer, and provide a sheltered spot since late flowers and foliage can be damaged by an early hard freeze.

planting.note: Plant the small bulbil-like grains or divisions in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the rosettes can establish over winter before spring bloom.

directions: Meadow saxifrage grows from small grain-like bulbils clustered at the base of the stem, which give the species its name and let it persist through dry summer dormancy. In spring it sends up slender stems carrying clean white, cup-shaped flowers above a rosette of softly hairy, kidney-shaped leaves, then dies back and disappears below ground for the summer once flowering finishes. It suits a partially shaded spot at a woodland edge or meadow planting where its vanishing act in summer will not leave an obvious gap. Plant where soil is moist in spring but can dry out somewhat once the foliage withers, mimicking its native damp-meadow-to-dry-summer cycle.

common_name: Clarence Elliott London Pride (Compact Pink-Flowered Saxifrage)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing closely to form a solid mat.

directions: This named selection of London pride stays noticeably more compact than the typical hybrid, with smaller evergreen rosettes that knit into a dense, tidy mat. In late spring, wiry stems carry airy sprays of small, pink-flushed, star-shaped flowers held well above the foliage. Its smaller scale makes it a good fit for edging a shaded path or tucking into a rock garden crevice where the full-sized species would feel too coarse. Grow it the same way as other London pride forms, in humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates root competition and dry shade better than most flowering groundcovers.

common_name: Snow Carpet Mossy Saxifrage (White-Flowered Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the moss-like mat can knit together before summer heat arrives.

directions: Schneeteppich, German for snow carpet, forms a dense, mossy evergreen cushion of tiny lobed leaves that all but disappears beneath its spring flower show. Short stems held just above the foliage carry masses of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers so thick they can hide the foliage entirely for a couple of weeks. Like other mossy saxifrages it prefers cool roots and resents hot, humid summer conditions, so give it afternoon shade and well-drained soil that does not bake dry. It works well tucked between paving stones or along the edge of a shaded rock garden where its tight habit and brief but showy bloom can be appreciated up close.
